summary:
We built Pulso Verde, an interactive 3D globe for studying real land-change events: deforestation in Rondônia and the Argentine Chaco, the 2015 Borneo fires, Australia's Black Summer, and reforestation efforts in Ethiopia and Brazil's Atlantic Forest. For each event, a Python pipeline pulls monthly NASA data from 2001 to 2024 (GLDAS Noah 2.1 and MERRA-2 from GES DISC). It tracks four variables: vegetation, surface temperature, soil moisture and rainfall. A Vue web app then shows how each variable changed after the event.

This answers the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by going beyond describing a trend. We compare each event area with a nearby untouched region, measured against its normal conditions before the event. A change counts as clear only if it passes set statistical tests: more than 2 standard deviations, Welch's t-test, and lasting at least two months. The tool also estimates how many months each variable took, or may still take, to return to normal. Missing data is shown as unavailable, never filled with made-up values.

This matters because land-use decisions are often made without seeing their effects on climate and water. Pulso Verde lets anyone see whether a forest loss or a restoration effort measurably changed the local environment, and how long recovery takes.
details:
Pulso Verde: Earth System Trend Detective
What does it do and how does it work?
Pulso Verde is a web tool for evaluating real deforestation, wildfire and reforestation events. It shows how each event changed four Earth-system variables (vegetation, surface temperature, soil moisture and precipitation), whether the change is statistically clear, and how long each variable took (or will take) to recover.

You pick an event, such as the 2004 deforestation peak in Rondônia, the 2015 Kalimantan peatland fires, Australia's 2019–2020 "Black Summer," or Pakistan's Billion Tree Tsunami. There are eight events across South America, Asia, Africa and Oceania. Then:

An interactive 3D globe flies to the event and plays the change month by month. Each map shows how far each variable is from its pre-event normal.
The event is compared with a similar control region that had no major disturbance (for example, Rondônia is compared with intact forest in Amazonas). This separates the event's own effect from regional climate swings like El Niño.
A side panel explains the result in plain language: what changed, whether it is significant, and whether it has recovered. The test counts a change as clear if it goes beyond 2 standard deviations of the pre-event baseline and Welch's t-test gives p < 0.05, or if it lasts at least two months in a row. Recovery means returning to the normal band for two straight months. If a variable hasn't recovered yet, a trend line estimates how long it would take.
A News tab links real reporting about each event (NASA Earth Observatory, Mongabay, CIFOR, CSIRO and others).
A Simulate tab asks "what if X points of tree cover were cut or replanted?" It answers using lagged regressions learned from the real events, not from made-up rules.
Benefits
Clear cause and effect: comparing each event with a control region shows what changed because of the land-cover change, not just what changed.
Statistical honesty: results are labeled as association, not proof of cause, and missing data shows as "not available" instead of being filled in. We also test the method against itself (see "Factors we considered").
Easy to use: plain-language verdicts, no GIS software, no downloads, and a static site that runs in any browser.
Reproducible: every dataset is logged in SOURCES.csv with its product ID, layer, unit conversion and request URL. New events are added in one YAML file with no code changes.
Intended impact
We want students, journalists, local decision-makers and the public to see that cutting or burning a forest is not just a loss of trees. It shifts local temperature, soil moisture and rainfall, and recovery can take years. The reforestation cases (Atlantic Forest, Pakistan, Ethiopia) show the reverse: restoration has measurable benefits. By turning NASA data into a clear "what changed, and how long until it heals," we hope to support better conversations about land use, restoration funding and fire management.

Tools, languages, hardware and software
Frontend: JavaScript, Vue 3, Vite, Pinia, and d3 with TopoJSON / world-atlas for the canvas globe. All statistics (Welch's t-test, incomplete-beta p-values, trend fits) are written from scratch in JavaScript.
Data pipeline: Python 3.11 with earthaccess, xarray, netCDF4, numpy, geopandas, pyyaml and pytest.
NASA data: GLDAS Noah 2.1 monthly at 0.25° (soil moisture, air temperature, rainfall) and MERRA-2 land monthly (vegetation greenness), both from GES DISC via Earthdata Login, covering 2001–2024. Planned next: MODIS tree cover and land surface temperature (via AppEEARS), GPM IMERG precipitation (via Giovanni), and NOAA CDO station data for checking results.
Testing: Node's test runner checks the analysis against a reference set of known answers, pytest covers the pipeline, plus a validation script and a link checker for the News tab.
Hardware: ordinary personal laptops (Windows). No special hardware or paid cloud services.
AI assistance: we used Claude Code as a coding assistant for porting and implementation, working from specifications and design decisions the team wrote (docs/, DECISIONS.md).
How is the project creative?
It's about events, not just trends. Most trend explorers show "the planet got warmer." We ask a specific question: this forest was cleared or burned or replanted, so what happened to its climate, and has it recovered?
Recovery time as the headline. Turning statistics into "recovered in about 3 years" or "still about 5 years away" makes the science easy to grasp.
A simulator that learns from real data. Its responses come from patterns in the real events, so it stays tied to observations.
Same variable, opposite directions. Deforestation and reforestation side by side show that one variable can rise in one place and fall in another. This is one of the challenge's key ideas.
Science plus stories: each satellite result sits next to news coverage of the people and places affected.
Factors our team considered
Data sources: we use only the sources the organizers allowed, with one main source per variable and an independent cross-check where possible.
Statistical rigor and honesty: we run placebo tests with fake event years and baseline-sensitivity tests (4 vs. 6 years). The current placebo false-positive rate (20%, mostly temperature) is above our 10% target, so we are tightening the criterion equally for all events. We report this openly in docs/VALIDATION.md rather than hiding it.
Control regions: each one is chosen for a similar ecosystem and no major disturbance. Some are marked "provisional" until higher-resolution tree-cover data confirms them.
Data size and cost: we fetch only what each event box needs, process each file as soon as it downloads, then delete the raw data and keep the job ID and checksum for reproducibility.
Accessibility and language: everyday wording, a consistent color palette, links that open a specific event and variable, and a fast globe (the detailed coastline is drawn only when the view is still).
Limits of satellite data: sparse ground stations in the Amazon, the Chaco and Borneo, the difference between air temperature and surface temperature, and the fact that correlation is not causation.
